topics.title: Accountability Foundations: Top-of-License Practice, Autonomy, Governance & the Five Components
topics.summary: Accountability means a nurse answers for the judgments, actions, and omissions of their practice; it rests on five professional components—education, a body of knowledge, service orientation, allegiance to a code of ethics, and autonomy through professional organization—and on practicing at the top of one’s license.
objectives: Distinguish accountability from responsibility, authority, and liability, and apply the difference to bedside situations.
Explain top-of-license (TOL) practice and identify nursing actions that reflect practicing to the full extent of education and legal scope.
Compare professional (collective) autonomy with individual (clinical) autonomy and recognize the limits of each.
Describe how governance—boards of nursing, professional organizations, and shared governance—gives nurses control over practice, discipline, and working conditions.
Apply the five components that promote professional accountability to realistic professional scenarios.
Select the nursing action that best demonstrates accountability when a situation pits convenience, cost, or hierarchy against client safety.
Identify where nursing standards come from (Nurse Practice Act, board rules, codes of ethics, facility policy) and which one governs in a given situation.
topics.bigPicture:
Accountability is the word nursing uses for one simple promise: “I will answer for what I do, what I decide, and what I fail to do.” Every time you sign a medication administration record, accept a client assignment, delegate a task, or decide a finding is “probably nothing,” you are making a decision you can be asked to explain—to the client, the charge nurse, the provider, your employer, the board of nursing, and sometimes a court. Accountability is not about blame. It is about ownership: being able to say what you assessed, why you acted, what happened next, and what you did about it.

This concept sits underneath almost every Management of Care item on the NCLEX. When a question asks what the nurse should do when a provider’s order seems unsafe, when a client says “I’m fine” but looks otherwise, when a colleague cuts a corner, or when a task is delegated and goes wrong, the exam is testing whether you understand that the registered nurse cannot hand accountability to someone else. You can delegate tasks; you cannot delegate your judgment or your answerability for the outcome.

This lesson builds the foundation: what accountability is, how it differs from look-alike words, what top-of-license practice means, how autonomy and governance let nursing regulate itself, and the five components that make nursing a profession whose members are accountable. Master these ideas and the application questions in the next two topics—bedside duties, delegation, unsafe orders, and competence—become much easier to reason through.

keyTerms.def: Being answerable—to the client, the profession, the employer, and the law—for one’s own nursing judgments, actions, and omissions and for their outcomes; it cannot be transferred to another person.

The duty or obligation to carry out a task or role (for example, the assigned tasks of a shift); a person can be given a responsibility, but the professional nurse remains accountable for how the work is carried out and evaluated.

An interprofessional approach to care delivery that enables nurses (the course emphasizes BSN or higher) to practice to the fullest extent of their education, knowledge, skills, and legal scope. Rooted in the IOM (2010) report The Future of Nursing: Leading Change, Advancing Health, it includes eight core nursing responsibilities—such as outcomes-focused care and facilitation of safe patient transitions—and requires nurses to be accountable in practice and to advocate for their own and colleagues’ autonomy.

The profession’s independence to self-regulate: setting standards of practice for its members, formulating nursing policy, and holding legal authority—vested in state boards of nursing—to define its goals, roles, and scope of practice.

The individual nurse’s professional responsibility, accountability for their own actions, and freedom to perform clinical duties as necessary within scope while advocating for safe, evidence-based care.

The organizational structure provided by a professional nursing organization that establishes and maintains social, political, and economic arrangements, giving professionals the means to control their professional affairs, including their practice, self-discipline, and working conditions.

A facility-level model in which bedside nurses share decision-making authority (through councils or committees) with managers about practice standards, quality, staffing, and professional development.

Entry into U.S. RN practice requires completing an approved nursing program (hospital diploma, associate degree [ADN], or bachelor’s degree [BSN]; some enter through entry-level master’s programs) and passing the NCLEX-RN. The ANA recommends the BSN for entry into professional practice, and Magnet hospitals require BSN-prepared nurses in leadership and strongly favor BSN preparation.

Nursing’s distinct, continuously expanding knowledge and expertise built on conceptual nursing frameworks and ongoing research; nurses apply it through evidence-based practice (EBP) to promote safe care.

Nursing’s commitment to serving others rather than profit, guided by tradition, accountability, rules, policies, and codes of ethics—for example, volunteering in the Medical Reserve Corps during a crisis such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

keyTerms.term: Allegiance to a code of ethics (component 4)
keyTerms.def: Commitment to the profession’s code (in the U.S., the ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses): respecting the inherent worth and dignity of every person and doing what is right, even at personal cost, to maintain moral integrity.

keyTerms.term: Autonomy & membership in a professional organization (component 5)
keyTerms.def: Practicing within professional organizations that provide governance, self-regulation, and legal and clinical autonomy for the profession.
Integrating the best current research evidence with clinical expertise and the client’s values and preferences to make care decisions.
The state law that defines nursing, sets the legal scope of practice, and creates the state board of nursing, which licenses nurses and disciplines those who violate the act or its rules.
A credential from the American Nurses Credentialing Center (ANCC) recognizing nursing excellence, strong nursing outcomes, and professional practice environments such as shared governance.

sections.heading: Accountability, responsibility, authority, and liability: four words the NCLEX expects you to separate
sections.body:
Students often treat these as synonyms. They are not, and many exam questions hinge on the difference. Responsibility is the duty to do something—“you are responsible for passing the 0900 medications.” Authority is the legitimate power to act or direct others, granted by law (your license) and by your employer (your position). Accountability is being answerable for how the duty was carried out and for its results, including what you did not do. Liability is legal responsibility for harm, decided by courts or regulators after the fact.

Here is why the difference matters: responsibility for a task can be shared or handed off, but accountability for nursing judgment stays with the licensed nurse who made the decision. When an RN asks a nursing assistant to obtain vital signs, the assistant becomes responsible for measuring and reporting them accurately—and is accountable for that performance—while the RN remains accountable for deciding the delegation was appropriate, giving clear directions, interpreting the results, and acting on them. If the RN never looks at the numbers, “I delegated it” is not a defense.

Accountability also runs in several directions at once: to the client (primary commitment), to yourself (moral integrity and competence), to the profession (standards and code of ethics), to the employer (policies and procedures), and to society through the law and the board of nursing. When those pulls conflict—for example, a policy shortcut that saves time but endangers a client—the client’s safety and the professional standard win.

check.q: An RN asks a nursing assistant to check a postoperative client’s blood pressure. The assistant records 84/50 in the electronic record but tells no one. Two hours later the client is found hypotensive and drowsy. Who was accountable for acting on the reading?
check.a: Both share parts of it, but the RN remains accountable for following up on delegated data. The assistant was responsible (and accountable) for reporting an abnormal value as directed; the RN was accountable for giving clear reporting parameters, supervising, reviewing the result, and acting. Delegation transfers the task, not the RN’s accountability for the outcome.

sections.heading: Top-of-license practice: doing everything your education and license allow
sections.body:
Top-of-license (TOL) practice grew out of the Institute of Medicine’s 2010 report The Future of Nursing: Leading Change, Advancing Health, which recommended that nurses practice to the full extent of their education and training. TOL is an interprofessional approach: every member of the team works at the highest level their preparation and legal scope allow, so that licensed nurses are not consumed by tasks someone else could safely do while the work only a nurse can do—assessment, clinical judgment, care coordination, teaching, evaluation—goes undone.

The course describes eight core nursing responsibilities within TOL practice, highlighting outcomes-focused care and facilitating safe patient transitions (handoffs, transfers, and discharges). In practice, a nurse working at the top of license is the one who notices a subtle trend, coordinates the dietitian and the pharmacist, teaches a client to recognize warning signs before discharge, and follows up the next day. TOL also carries an advocacy duty: nurses must be accountable in practice and must advocate for their own and their colleagues’ autonomy—for example, speaking up when a staffing model reduces RNs to task completion and leaves no time for assessment.

TOL does not mean doing whatever you want. The “top” is defined by two ceilings at once: your legal scope (the Nurse Practice Act and board rules) and your personal competence (what you have been educated and validated to do safely). Practicing at the top of license is the opposite of practicing beyond it.
sections.example: A medical-surgical RN spends the first hour of every shift restocking supply carts because no one else does it. Meanwhile, two clients go without a timely reassessment after receiving opioids. A TOL-minded nurse raises the issue through the unit practice council, proposes that unlicensed staff handle restocking, and protects RN time for reassessment and discharge teaching—work that only the RN can do.

check.q: Which action best reflects top-of-license practice: (a) personally passing every meal tray so clients eat on time, or (b) coordinating a family meeting and discharge teaching for a client going home with a new insulin regimen?
check.a: (b). Coordinating a safe transition and teaching are core RN functions requiring nursing judgment. Passing trays is valuable but can be done by others; spending licensed time on it while RN-only work waits is the opposite of TOL practice.

sections.heading: Autonomy at two levels: the profession and the person
sections.body:
Autonomy means independence or freedom, and in nursing it exists at two levels that work together. Professional autonomy belongs to nursing as a whole: the profession regulates itself, sets standards of practice for its members, formulates nursing policy, and—through the legal authority vested in state boards of nursing—defines its own goals, roles, and scope of practice. Nurses, not hospital administrators, write the standards that define safe nursing care.

Individual autonomy belongs to you at the bedside. It means professional responsibility, accountability for your own actions, and the freedom to perform clinical duties as necessary—initiating independent nursing interventions such as repositioning, teaching, comfort measures, and escalation—while advocating for safe, evidence-based care. Autonomy is why a nurse can hold a medication when the client’s respiratory rate is 8 and notify the provider; it is also why that nurse must be able to justify the decision.

Autonomy and accountability are two sides of the same coin. The more freedom you have to make decisions, the more you must answer for them. A nurse who wants the independence to make judgments but avoids documenting or explaining them misunderstands the bargain. On the NCLEX, autonomy rarely appears as a definition; it appears as an option in which the nurse independently takes an appropriate nursing action within scope (for example, holding a dose and reassessing) instead of waiting passively for permission.

sections.analogy: Think of a professional sports league. The league (the profession) writes the rulebook and disciplines players who break it—that is professional autonomy. Each player (the nurse) decides in the moment how to play within those rules and must answer for the play they made—that is individual autonomy. A player cannot claim freedom to ignore the rulebook, and the league cannot play the game for the player.

check.q: A client’s respiratory rate is 9/min and they are difficult to arouse 45 minutes after an opioid dose. The next scheduled dose is due. Which response shows individual autonomy exercised accountably?
check.a: Withhold the dose, stimulate and reassess the client (airway, breathing, sedation level, SpO2), follow protocol for opioid-induced respiratory depression, notify the provider, and document. Holding a dose for a safety finding is an independent nursing judgment within scope; failing to explain or report it would not be accountable.

sections.heading: Governance: how nurses control their own practice, discipline, and working conditions
sections.body:
Governance is the organizational structure that gives professionals the means to control their professional affairs. The course frames it as structure provided by professional nursing organizations that establishes and maintains social, political, and economic arrangements—the machinery that lets nurses influence their practice, their self-discipline, and their working conditions rather than having those dictated entirely by others.

Governance shows up at several levels. At the state level, the Nurse Practice Act creates a board of nursing that licenses nurses, writes rules, and disciplines nurses whose conduct endangers the public. At the national level, the National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN) is an organization of boards that develops the NCLEX and model regulatory guidance (for example, national delegation guidelines), and the American Nurses Association (ANA) publishes the Code of Ethics for Nurses and the scope and standards of practice. Specialty organizations publish specialty standards. At the facility level, shared governance councils let bedside nurses help decide practice policies, quality projects, and staffing approaches.

Why does this matter for a student? Because questions about “who decides” are really questions about governance. The board of nursing decides what is legal for a nurse to do. A facility policy can make practice more restrictive than the law, but it can never authorize a nurse to do what the Nurse Practice Act prohibits. Professional organizations set ethical and practice standards that courts use to judge the “reasonable and prudent nurse.” And shared governance is the accountable route for changing a unit practice you disagree with—bring evidence to the practice council rather than quietly ignoring the policy.

check.q: A unit’s informal custom is for RNs to co-sign controlled-substance wastes they did not witness “to save time.” A new nurse thinks the custom is unsafe. What is the most accountable route?
check.a: Refuse to co-sign a waste she did not witness (that is falsification and a diversion risk), follow the controlled-substance policy, and raise the custom with the charge nurse/manager and through shared governance or the practice council. Governance structures exist so nurses can fix practice problems openly rather than comply with unsafe norms.

sections.heading: The five components that promote professional accountability
sections.body:
The course identifies five components that make nursing a profession whose members are accountable. Learn them as a set, but more importantly learn what each one looks like in behavior, because the exam will describe the behavior and ask you to recognize the principle or choose the action that fits it. For each component below, read the definition, then the “how you will see it” line: that line is what an exam stem will actually describe.

1. Education. Entry into U.S. RN practice requires completing an approved program and passing the NCLEX-RN. Programs include the hospital diploma, the associate degree (ADN), and the bachelor’s degree (BSN); master’s and doctoral degrees (MSN, DNP, PhD) prepare nurses for advanced and leadership roles. The ANA recommends the BSN for entry into professional practice, Magnet hospitals require BSN preparation for nurse leaders and strongly favor BSN-prepared staff, and many ADN nurses advance through RN-to-BSN programs. How you will see it: a nurse enrolls in an RN-to-BSN program, earns a specialty certification, or completes required continuing education.

2. Body of knowledge. Nursing has a distinct, continuously expanding body of knowledge built on conceptual nursing frameworks and research. Nurses are accountable for applying it through evidence-based practice rather than “the way we have always done it.” How you will see it: a nurse looks up current evidence before changing a routine, or questions a practice that newer guidelines no longer support.

3. Service orientation. Unlike profit-driven occupations, nursing prioritizes service to others, guided by tradition, accountability, rules, policies, and codes of ethics. Nurses who volunteered in state and national Medical Reserve Corps during the COVID-19 pandemic—helping health departments with data collection, phone banks, and public health information—illustrate this component. How you will see it: a nurse puts the needs of clients or the community ahead of personal gain or convenience (volunteering in a crisis, staying to give a complete handoff). Paid overtime for extra income is employment, not service orientation.

4. Allegiance to a code of ethics. Nurses respect the inherent worth and dignity of every person and do what is right even at personal cost, to maintain moral integrity. How you will see it: a nurse reports her own error, declines to co-sign a waste she did not witness, or reports an impaired friend, even though it is uncomfortable.

5. Autonomy and membership in a professional organization. Professional organizations provide governance, self-regulation, and legal and clinical autonomy; belonging to and participating in them is how nurses shape the standards they are held to. How you will see it: a nurse joins a professional or specialty association, serves on a standards committee, or sits on the unit practice council.

Step-by-step for a “which component?” item: (1) Underline the behavior in the stem. (2) Ask what motivates it: learning (education), evidence (body of knowledge), serving others ahead of self (service), doing right at personal cost (ethics), or shaping professional standards (organization/autonomy). (3) Watch for traps: habit is not body of knowledge, and paid work is not service orientation.

check.q: A nurse discovers she gave a client the wrong dose of a medication. No harm is apparent, and no one else noticed. Which component of accountability most directly requires her to assess the client, notify the provider, and file an event report?
check.a: Allegiance to a code of ethics—doing what is right even at personal cost to maintain moral integrity. (Her immediate actions are also clinical accountability: assess the client first, then notify and report per policy.)

sections.heading: Education and the body of knowledge: why “the way we have always done it” is not a defense
sections.body:
Accountability is impossible without knowledge. A nurse cannot answer for a decision she cannot explain, and an explanation must rest on something more than habit. This is why education (component 1) and the body of knowledge (component 2) are listed first. Initial education qualifies you to sit for the NCLEX; ongoing education keeps you safe as evidence changes. The body of knowledge is “continuously expanding”—which means some of what you learn in school will be outdated within a few years.

Evidence-based practice is how the body of knowledge reaches the bedside. EBP integrates three things: the best available research evidence, the nurse’s clinical expertise, and the client’s values and preferences. In general, systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials provide the strongest evidence, followed by individual randomized trials, then well-designed nonrandomized and observational studies, then qualitative and descriptive studies, with expert opinion and committee reports at the base. Clinical practice guidelines from professional bodies translate that evidence into recommendations.

On the exam, EBP accountability usually appears in two forms. First, a unit routine conflicts with current evidence—the accountable action is to look for and bring evidence to the appropriate group (practice council, educator, EBP committee) rather than either blindly continuing or unilaterally changing the policy. Second, an order conflicts with current evidence or the client’s condition—the accountable action is to clarify with the prescriber (you will practice this in the next topic). Either way, accountability means acting on knowledge through legitimate channels.
sections.example: A nurse notices that the unit still uses a skin-prep routine that a newer guideline no longer recommends. Accountable practice is not to quietly use her own method on her clients, and not to keep using the outdated routine without comment. She searches the literature, brings a summary to the unit practice council, and asks the nurse educator to review the policy—EBP through governance.

check.q: Which statement by a nurse best demonstrates accountability for the body of knowledge? (a) “I learned this in school ten years ago, so it is still right.” (b) “Our policy says to do it this way, but let me check whether the evidence has changed and bring it to the practice council.”
check.a: (b). It respects current policy while using EBP and governance to update practice. Statement (a) treats knowledge as fixed, which contradicts nursing’s continuously expanding body of knowledge.

sections.heading: Service orientation and the code of ethics: doing right when it costs something
sections.body:
Service orientation means nursing exists to serve the public, not primarily to earn profit. That does not mean nurses must work without pay or ignore their own well-being; it means that when service and self-interest conflict, the nurse’s professional obligation to the client and community carries great weight. Rules, policies, and codes of ethics give this service a structure so that it is reliable rather than dependent on individual mood.

Allegiance to a code of ethics is where accountability gets personal. The ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses establishes that the nurse’s primary commitment is to the client, that the nurse protects the client’s health, safety, and rights, and that the nurse is accountable for their own judgments and actions. The course puts it bluntly: nurses must do what is right “even at personal cost” to maintain moral integrity. Personal cost might be an uncomfortable conversation with a senior physician, admitting your own error, staying a few minutes late to give a complete handoff, or reporting an impaired colleague who is also a friend.

A note on who writes the code: the ANA, a professional organization, publishes the U.S. Code of Ethics for Nurses. State boards of nursing enforce the law; they can discipline unprofessional or unsafe conduct that also violates ethical standards, and the NCSBN coordinates the boards, but it is the profession itself that authors its ethical code. That is exactly what professional autonomy means.
sections.example: At the end of a 12-hour shift, a nurse realizes she never completed the neurovascular checks ordered every 2 hours on a client with a new cast. She is tired and the next shift has arrived. The accountable action is to perform (or ensure the oncoming nurse immediately performs) the check, document accurately with the actual time, report the missed checks to the charge nurse, and include them in the handoff—not to chart the checks as if they had been done.

check.q: A nurse’s close friend and coworker smells of alcohol and is slurring words while preparing medications. Which action reflects allegiance to the code of ethics?
check.a: Protect clients first: prevent the coworker from providing care (do not let her continue with medications) and immediately notify the charge nurse or supervisor per policy so she is removed from duty and the situation is reported appropriately. Friendship does not outweigh the primary commitment to client safety.

sections.body: These pairs cause most wrong answers on accountability items. When two options look similar, find the clue in the stem that separates them.

If the question is “who must follow up / answer for the result,” it is the RN who delegated or decided.

If the client is deciding about their own care, the principle is client autonomy (self-determination).

If the action needs a medical order or skill the nurse lacks, it is not TOL—it is out of scope.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: recognizing accountable professional behavior
sections.body:
The NCLEX almost never asks, “What is the definition of accountability?” Instead it shows you a nurse in a situation and asks which action, statement, or behavior best demonstrates accountability, autonomy, or professional practice—or which statement by a new nurse needs further teaching. The wrong options are usually behaviors that sound efficient, polite, or loyal but shift answerability to someone else (“I’ll let the provider decide”), hide information (“no harm was done, so I won’t report it”), or follow habit over evidence.

Use three filters. Filter 1: Who owns it? The correct option keeps the licensed nurse answerable for judgment and follow-up. Filter 2: Is it honest and transparent? Accountable options disclose, document accurately, and report through proper channels. Filter 3: Does it put the client first within scope? Accountable options protect the client without stepping outside legal scope. Work through the sample item below with those filters.
steps: Read the stem: “A nurse realizes that she forgot to give a client’s 0900 dose of an oral antihypertensive; it is now 1300 and the client’s blood pressure is 168/96. Which action by the nurse best demonstrates accountability?” Options: (A) Give the dose now and chart it as given at 0900. (B) Assess the client, notify the provider of the omission and current BP, follow the provider’s direction, document accurately, and complete an event report. (C) Wait until the next scheduled dose and give a double dose. (D) Ask the oncoming nurse to decide how to handle it.
Identify what is being asked: the behavior that best shows accountability—owning an omission and its outcome.
Spot the cues: a missed dose (an omission is still the nurse’s accountability), an elevated BP (a possible consequence requiring assessment), and the word “best.”
Eliminate (A): giving the dose late may or may not be appropriate, but charting it as given at 0900 is falsification—never accountable.
Eliminate (C): doubling a dose is unsafe and is a medication decision outside nursing scope without an order.
Eliminate (D): passing the decision to someone else shifts accountability away from the nurse who made the error.
Choose (B): it assesses first, discloses honestly, obtains direction within scope, documents truthfully, and reports through the system so the error can be learned from.

Reusable strategy: when an option involves hiding, delaying, or handing off ownership, eliminate it. The accountable answer usually contains assess → act within scope → communicate → document → report/follow up.

sections.heading: Worked case: the new graduate, the outdated routine, and the missed reassessment
sections.body:
Marcus is an RN six months out of school on a busy surgical unit. During his shift he notices three things. First, an older nurse tells him the unit always irrigates certain drains with a solution and frequency that Marcus remembers reading is no longer recommended by current guidance. Second, he gave a client an IV opioid at 1400 for pain rated 8/10 and, because of an admission, did not reassess until 1520. The client is comfortable and breathing normally, with a pain rating of 3/10. Third, during a staff huddle, the manager asks for volunteers to serve on the unit’s new shared-governance practice council.

Marcus wants to do the right thing but also wants to fit in. Let’s reason through each issue the way an accountable nurse—and the NCLEX—would.
steps: Recognize cues: (1) a unit routine may conflict with current evidence; (2) a reassessment after an IV opioid was late (an omission, even though the outcome was good); (3) an opportunity to participate in governance.

Analyze the drain routine: Marcus is accountable for practicing within an EBP environment, but he is also bound by policy. He should not unilaterally change care on his own clients; instead he verifies the current policy and the order, searches for current evidence, and brings it to the educator or practice council.

Analyze the late reassessment: accountability covers omissions. Reassessment after an IV opioid is expected within the time frame set by policy (commonly about 15–30 minutes for IV). Marcus reassesses now, documents the actual time and findings accurately, and follows his facility’s process for reporting a delayed reassessment if policy requires it. He also reflects on what caused the delay so he can prevent it—for example, asking the charge nurse for help when an admission conflicts with a required reassessment.

Analyze the council invitation: joining is not required, but it is a direct expression of component 5 (autonomy and membership in professional governance) and the advocacy duty within top-of-license practice. It is also the legitimate forum for the drain-irrigation question.
Take action: Marcus documents truthfully, tells the charge nurse about the late reassessment, volunteers for the council, and brings the drain evidence to its first meeting.

Evaluate outcomes: The client stayed safe; the record is accurate; the unit has a pathway to review an outdated routine; and Marcus has learned to delegate or ask for help when competing demands threaten a required reassessment.

check.q: If the client had been sedated with a respiratory rate of 8 at 1520, how would Marcus’s priorities change?
check.a: Client safety comes first: stay with the client, stimulate and support breathing, follow the opioid-reversal protocol/rapid response as indicated, and notify the provider—then document and report. Event reporting and reflection follow stabilization; they never precede emergency care.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
In North Carolina, nursing is regulated by the North Carolina Board of Nursing (NCBON) under the Nursing Practice Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 90, Article 9A, G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.). The Board’s rules describe the components of practice for the RN in 21 NCAC 36 .0224 and for the LPN in 21 NCAC 36 .0225. Under these rules, the RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment; the LPN participates in care under the supervision of an RN or other authorized provider. The RN may delegate tasks but not the nursing process or nursing judgment.

NCBON publishes a scope-of-practice decision tree to help a nurse decide whether an activity is within his or her scope, and a Decision Tree for Delegation to UAP. North Carolina is a Nurse Licensure Compact state, so a nurse whose primary state of residence is NC may hold a multistate license and practice in other compact states—while remaining accountable to the Nurse Practice Act of the state where the client is located.

For practice events, NCBON uses a Just Culture–based Complaint Evaluation Tool that distinguishes human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior. Conduct issues—drug diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary or sexual misconduct, and confidentiality breaches—are reported to the Board rather than handled only by the employer. NCBON also offers alternative-to-discipline programs for nurses with substance use disorders. You will apply these ideas in the next topic.
bullets: NCLEX is national and will not ask NC statute numbers; use these facts for practice in NC.
Facility policy can be stricter than 21 NCAC 36 .0224/.0225 but never broader.
When unsure whether an act is within scope, use the NCBON scope-of-practice decision tree and agency policy before acting.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Source: Module 42 study guide, Glossary terms 1–3 (Top-of-License Practice, Autonomy, Governance) and “The Concept of Accountability & Its Five Core Components,” pp. 2703–2704. National content added for NCLEX context: accountability vs responsibility vs authority vs liability, shared governance, the roles of the board of nursing/NCSBN/ANA, and a brief hierarchy of evidence.
bullets: Entry pathways: the course lists diploma, ADN, BSN, MSN, and DNP/PhD programs. Clarification: initial RN licensure is through a diploma, ADN, BSN, or an entry-level (direct-entry) master’s program plus the NCLEX-RN; the MSN, DNP, and PhD are otherwise graduate degrees for advanced practice, education, leadership, and research.

Codes of ethics: the course says nursing’s codes are “regulated alongside state boards of nursing via the NCSBN.” Clarification: the ANA (a professional organization) authors the U.S. Code of Ethics for Nurses; state boards enforce the Nurse Practice Act and may discipline conduct that also violates ethical standards; the NCSBN is the association of boards that develops the NCLEX and model regulatory guidance.

Magnet: Magnet recognition (ANCC) requires BSN or higher preparation for nurse managers and leaders and expects organizations to increase BSN-prepared staff; it does not require every staff RN to hold a BSN.

Top-of-license practice: the course frames TOL around BSN-prepared nurses. Every licensed nurse is expected to practice to the full extent of his or her own education, competence, and legal scope. The IOM is now the National Academy of Medicine, and its follow-up report, The Future of Nursing 2020–2030, extends these recommendations to health equity.

mnemonics.name: “E-B-S-C-A” — Every Brave Student Can Achieve (the five components)
mnemonics.text: Education • Body of knowledge • Service orientation • Code of ethics • Autonomy & professional organization.

mnemonics.name: Accountable answer pattern: A-A-C-D-R
mnemonics.text: Assess → Act within scope → Communicate (provider/charge nurse) → Document truthfully → Report/follow up. Options that skip or reverse these, hide information, or hand off ownership are usually wrong.

pearls: You can delegate a task; you can never delegate accountability for your nursing judgment or for following up.
Omissions count. A missed assessment, an unreported finding, or a skipped reassessment is part of what you are accountable for.
Facility policy can narrow your scope but never expand it beyond the Nurse Practice Act.
Autonomy comes bundled with answerability: the freedom to decide includes the duty to explain and document the decision.
Top-of-license means the full extent of your legal scope AND your personal competence—never beyond either.
The accountable way to change a practice you disagree with is through evidence and governance (practice council, educator, chain of command), not quiet noncompliance.
The primary commitment is to the client, even when that commitment costs you comfort, time, or popularity.
redFlags: Charting care that was not done, or charting it at a false time, is falsification—never an acceptable way to “fix” an omission.
Co-signing a controlled-substance waste you did not witness breaks accountability and enables diversion.
Letting a colleague who appears impaired continue to care for clients violates the primary commitment to client safety.
Assuming a delegated task was done correctly without reviewing results leaves the client unprotected and the RN accountable.
Following a routine “because we have always done it” when you have reason to believe it is unsafe—without raising it—is a failure of accountability.
recap: Accountability = answering for your judgments, actions, omissions, and outcomes; responsibility = the duty to do a task.
Top-of-license practice uses the full extent of a nurse’s education and legal scope, focusing on outcomes and safe transitions, and includes advocating for nurses’ autonomy.
Professional autonomy is the profession’s self-regulation; individual autonomy is the nurse’s freedom to act within scope—both demand accountability.
Governance (boards, professional organizations, shared governance) gives nurses control over practice, self-discipline, and working conditions.
The five components: education, body of knowledge, service orientation, allegiance to a code of ethics, and autonomy through professional organization.
Evidence-based practice is how nursing’s expanding body of knowledge reaches the bedside—through legitimate channels.
The accountable answer pattern: assess, act within scope, communicate, document truthfully, and report/follow up.

checks.q: A charge nurse tells a new RN, “Don’t bother filing an event report for that near miss—nothing happened.” What is the accountable response?
checks.a: Explain respectfully that near misses are reported so the system can learn and prevent future harm, and complete the event report per policy. Accountability and a culture of safety apply to near misses, not just to harm events.

checks.q: An LPN asks an RN to sign off a client’s admission assessment the LPN completed alone, saying, “You’re busy; I’ve done hundreds of these.” Why should the RN decline to simply sign it?
checks.a: The comprehensive admission assessment and the nursing judgment it supports are RN accountabilities. The LPN may collect data, but the RN must personally assess and validate; signing work she did not do would misrepresent her accountability.

checks.q: A hospital policy permits RNs to adjust certain medication doses by protocol. A nurse from another state says her old hospital let nurses change doses “whenever it made sense.” What principle should guide the nurse now?
checks.a: Practice is governed by the Nurse Practice Act of the state where the client is and by current facility policy and protocols. A former employer’s custom does not expand scope; dose changes require an order or an approved protocol.

checks.q: Which of the five components is most directly shown when a nurse joins a specialty nursing association and serves on its standards committee?
checks.a: Autonomy and membership in a professional organization—participating in the governance that sets the standards nurses are held to.

checks.q: A nurse wants to practice at the top of her license. Which is a better example: performing a procedure she has observed once but never been checked off on, or coordinating the interprofessional discharge plan for a complex client?
checks.a: Coordinating the discharge plan. TOL is bounded by competence; performing an unvalidated procedure exceeds competence, whereas care coordination and safe transitions are core RN functions.

checks.q: Why is “I followed the provider’s order exactly” not always a complete defense?
checks.a: Because the nurse is independently accountable for his or her own judgment. If an order is unclear or unsafe for the client, the nurse must question it, clarify with the prescriber, and escalate if needed rather than carry it out mechanically.

topics.title: Accountability at the Bedside: Expanded Duties, Related Concepts, Delegation & Unsafe Orders
topics.summary: Accountability becomes concrete in daily duties—comfort, safety, infection prevention, teaching, trauma and suicide screening, and evidence-based care—and in the decisions the RN cannot hand off: delegating and supervising, questioning unsafe orders, escalating through the chain of command, and owning errors.
objectives: Apply the expanded duties of accountability (holistic wellness, physical outcomes, safety, trauma/abuse/self-directed violence, education, infection prevention) to client scenarios.
Use the related-concepts matrix (comfort, EBP, health/wellness, infection, safety, teaching/learning, trauma) to choose the nursing implication a situation calls for.
Explain why the RN remains accountable after assigning or delegating, and apply the five rights of delegation.
Determine which tasks may be assigned to an LPN or delegated to assistive personnel and which must stay with the RN.
Carry out the steps for questioning an unsafe or outdated order and escalating through the chain of command.
Recognize mandatory reporting duties for suspected abuse, neglect, and specified injuries, and screen for suicide risk.
Respond to errors and near misses in a way consistent with accountability and Just Culture.
topics.bigPicture:
In the first topic, accountability was a principle. Here it becomes a set of things you actually do on a shift. The course lists the areas accountability governs: health and wellness, physical outcomes, safety, trauma and abuse reporting, suicide prevention, teaching, and infection control. Each one has concrete nursing implications—assess comfort at least every shift, screen every client for abuse and suicide risk at admission, wear the right PPE, assess readiness to learn before teaching, report safety concerns through the proper channel. When one of these is skipped, the nurse is answerable for the omission.

This topic also covers the decisions that test accountability under pressure. A client says “I’m fine” while gripping the sheets and shaking. An LPN throws away urine that was supposed to be strained for a kidney stone. An order calls for 500 mL/hr of IV fluid for a 78-year-old when current evidence and the client’s risk say that may be unsafe. A provider refuses to change an order the nurse believes will harm the client. In every case, the RN must act—assess, clarify, communicate, escalate, document—rather than defer, acquiesce, or assume someone else will catch it.

On the NCLEX this content shows up as delegation and assignment questions, “which action should the nurse take first” questions about unsafe orders, mandatory-reporting questions, and “best response” questions about clients who refuse care. The thread connecting them is the same: the registered nurse stays accountable for the client’s outcome, even when someone else performed the task or wrote the order.

keyTerms.def: The areas the nurse answers for: holistic health and wellness, physical patient outcomes, patient safety, trauma/abuse/self-directed violence, patient and self-education, and infection prevention and immunity.

The nurse is accountable for assessing comfort levels and providing effective interventions to promote and maintain comfort—assessing at least once per shift or more often per condition, reporting deviations, and documenting comfort level and every intervention.

The nurse is accountable for assessing biophysical, cognitive, psychologic, and spiritual health; teaching general health promotion and risk-specific lifestyle change; and referring to counselors, clergy, dietitians, physical therapists, support groups, and community resources.

The nurse is accountable for protecting clients whose immune systems are compromised by assessing for immunocompromised states, using PPE, knowing transmission mechanisms, and educating the public on immunization and hygiene.

The nurse is accountable for keeping clients safe in the healthcare setting and teaching risk reduction for daily life: addressing immediate hazards, assessing injury risk outside the setting, reporting safety concerns per policy, and teaching prevention (helmets, child safety restraints).

The nurse is accountable for client education across all care aspects, for staying current with evidence, and for guiding preceptees and students—assessing learning needs and readiness, designing EBP-based teaching, and maintaining competence through continuing education.

The nurse is accountable for recognizing signs of trauma, abuse, or violence, preventing further harm, and fulfilling mandatory reporting duties, including screening for abuse risk and suicide risk on admission.

A legal duty to report known or suspected abuse or neglect of children and of older or disabled adults, and specified injuries (such as gunshot wounds) as defined by state statute, to the designated agency.
An infection a client acquires while receiving care in a healthcare setting that was not present or incubating on admission.

Allowing a delegatee (usually assistive personnel) to perform a specific nursing activity, skill, or procedure that is beyond the delegatee’s traditional role and not routinely performed, while the delegating nurse retains accountability for the decision and the outcome.

Directing an individual to perform activities that are within that person’s authorized scope of practice (e.g., LPN) or routine role functions (e.g., UAP); the assigning RN remains accountable for appropriate assignment and supervision.
Right task, right circumstance, right person, right directions and communication, and right supervision and evaluation.
Providing guidance, direction, oversight, evaluation, and follow-up for tasks performed by others.
Trained, unlicensed workers (e.g., nursing assistants, patient care technicians) who perform delegated or assigned tasks under the supervision of a licensed nurse.
The organization’s established line of authority used to escalate an unresolved concern—e.g., prescriber → charge nurse → nursing supervisor/manager → medical director or chief nursing officer.

A medication order in which the dose (or frequency) varies within a prescribed range (e.g., hydromorphone 1–4 mg IV PRN); the nurse selects the dose based on assessment and policy and is accountable for the choice and for monitoring.
A confidential quality-improvement document describing an error, near miss, or unexpected occurrence; it is not placed in or referenced in the client’s medical record.
A safety framework that distinguishes human error (console), at-risk behavior (coach), and reckless behavior (sanction), holding individuals accountable for their choices while fixing system causes.

sections.heading: The expanded duties: what accountability covers on every shift
sections.body:
Accountability is foundational because it governs the essentials of nursing care. The course groups these into six duties. Holistic health and wellness: implementing preventive screenings, immunizations, smoking cessation, exercise, and healthy diets while addressing cognitive, psychologic, and spiritual health—stress management and referrals to counselors, clergy, or support groups. Physical patient outcomes: adequate fluids and nutrition, rest and sleep, appropriate oxygenation, elimination, and proactive assessment and management of pain and comfort. Patient safety: a hazard-free environment, injury-prevention teaching across the lifespan, and encouraging clients to voice concerns.

Trauma, abuse, and self-directed violence: nurses have a legal and ethical mandatory duty to report known or suspected abuse of children and older adults, and specified violence-related injuries such as gunshot wounds according to state statute. Nurses routinely screen all clients for abuse and assess for risk of self-harm, suicide, or suicidal ideation or intent. Patient and self-education: assess learning style and readiness to learn before teaching about health, illness, tests, procedures, diagnoses, treatments, and self-care—and keep your own knowledge current through continuing education and EBP. Infection prevention and immunity: nurses are on the front lines educating the public about immunization and preventing HAIs through self-awareness of personal exposure and strict infection control.

Notice the pattern: each duty has an assessment part (screen, assess, identify) and an action part (teach, intervene, refer, report, document). On the exam, the accountable answer often supplies the step that someone skipped—usually the assessment.

check.q: A nurse completes discharge teaching on new anticoagulant therapy for a client who is visibly drowsy after a sleepless night and says, “Just give me the papers.” Which accountability duty was not met?
check.a: Patient education—specifically assessing readiness to learn before teaching. The accountable plan is to reschedule or shorten teaching to essentials, include a support person if the client agrees, and confirm understanding with teach-back when the client is ready.

sections.heading: Comfort and the client who says “I’m fine”: lessons from Ms. Miller
sections.body:
The course’s first case shows how accountability works when words and cues disagree. Jen Sturges, a new RN, assesses Kathryn Miller, 45, admitted with a GI diagnosis and a history of back pain. Ms. Miller insists she is “doing just fine,” but her blood pressure is elevated, she is shaking and gripping the bed sheets, and she says she fears narcotics and “refuses to pay attention to my body.” She calls pain “my enemy.”

Jen’s first accountability is to complete the assessment before leaving the room. Elevated BP, shaking, and guarding are cues that a quick “Are you okay?” would miss. A complete assessment captures the baseline, prevents missed deterioration, and fulfills the nurse’s accountability for accurate data and comfort management. Jen should then share the specific findings with the charge nurse—elevated BP, nonverbal signs of severe pain, fear of opioid side effects, history of back pain, and the current GI diagnosis—so a safe, tailored plan can be coordinated with the provider or hospitalist, the clinical pharmacist (for non-opioid and multimodal analgesics compatible with her GI condition), and possibly a pain specialist or physical or integrative therapist.

Why not simply accept the refusal? A competent adult has the right to refuse an opioid, and the nurse respects that. But respecting a refusal is not the same as abandoning the problem. Untreated pain produces harmful physiologic stress responses—elevated blood pressure, impaired healing, heightened anxiety. Accountability requires the nurse to explore the client’s fears, correct misconceptions (for example, that short-term opioid use for acute pain almost always causes addiction), offer non-opioid and nonpharmacologic alternatives, and advocate for safe relief. Documentation must include the comfort level, the client’s stated reasons, the education given, and every intervention.
steps: Notice incongruence: the client’s words (“fine”) conflict with physiologic and behavioral cues (BP up, shaking, guarding).
Complete the assessment: pain characteristics using a scale and nonverbal indicators, vital signs, and the client’s beliefs and fears about treatment.
Explore and educate using therapeutic communication: “You mentioned you are afraid of narcotics. Tell me more about that.”
Collaborate: report findings to the charge nurse and provider; involve the pharmacist for multimodal or non-opioid options compatible with the GI diagnosis.
Offer choices the client accepts (nonpharmacologic measures, non-opioid analgesics, positioning, heat if ordered) and respect an informed refusal.
Reassess after each intervention and document comfort level, client statements, teaching, and interventions.

check.q: Ms. Miller declines all opioids after teaching. Which response is most accountable: documenting “client refuses pain medication” and checking back next shift, or offering alternatives and reassessing soon?
check.a: Offering ordered non-opioid and nonpharmacologic alternatives, notifying the provider about uncontrolled pain and the refusal so the plan can be adjusted, and reassessing soon. Documenting the refusal is necessary but does not by itself meet accountability for comfort.

sections.heading: Evidence-based practice at the bedside: questioning an order
sections.body:
The EBP row of the related-concepts matrix says the nurse is accountable for practicing within an EBP environment and for implementing evidence in personal practice: conducting literature searches for current evidence and selecting interventions grounded in the findings. The Epworth case makes this concrete. Frank Epworth, 78, is admitted with suspected urolithiasis, severe left flank pain, nausea and vomiting, and hematuria. Orders include hydromorphone (Dilaudid) 1–4 mg IV PRN pain, normal saline at 500 mL/hr, and straining all urine.

Shortly after starting the IV, the nurse recalls recent clinical guidance indicating that large-volume fluid pushes are rarely effective in helping stones pass. Add the client’s age—78—and the risk of fluid overload at 500 mL/hr, and the nurse now has both an evidence concern and a safety concern. Accountability does not permit ignoring the concern (“the provider ordered it”), and it does not permit the nurse to change the rate on her own. The accountable action is to assess the client (lung sounds, edema, intake and output, vital signs, cardiac and renal history), contact the prescriber promptly, share the client data and the current evidence, and advocate for a safer, evidence-supported rate.

This is the general rule for any order that seems inappropriate: clarify before you implement. If the prescriber changes the order, implement the new order and document the conversation. If the prescriber maintains an order the nurse believes is unsafe, the nurse does not carry it out, informs the prescriber, and escalates through the chain of command (covered below). Documentation is factual: who was notified, when, what was said, and what was done.
steps: Recognize the cue: an order conflicts with current evidence or with the client’s condition (age, cardiac or renal status, allergies, labs).
Assess the client for any current effect (for fluids: lung sounds, dyspnea, SpO2, edema, I&O, weight).
Gather the evidence: the current guideline or policy, drug reference, or pharmacist input.
Contact the prescriber using SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation (“I recommend reducing the rate to…”).
Implement the clarified order, or if the prescriber maintains an order that remains unsafe, withhold it, tell the prescriber, and escalate.
Document the facts and continue to monitor the client.

check.q: During the clarification call, the provider says, “Fine, run it at 150 mL/hr.” What must the nurse do next?
check.a: Follow facility policy for verbal/telephone orders (read back the order, have it entered/signed per policy), change the rate, document the communication, and reassess the client’s fluid status and pain. The nurse remains accountable for monitoring the response to the new rate.

sections.heading: Delegation and assignment: the task moves, the accountability stays
sections.body:
In the Epworth case, the RN gives hydromorphone and asks an LPN to collect and strain the client’s urine. Half an hour later the LPN reports that Mr. Epworth voided 30 mL five minutes ago, and the LPN charted it and discarded it without straining. Is the RN accountable for the LPN’s error? Yes. The LPN is accountable for performing the task correctly, but the RN retains overall accountability for client outcomes, for making an appropriate delegation or assignment, for communicating the critical instruction (strain all urine for stone analysis), and for supervising and evaluating the care.

National guidelines (NCSBN and ANA, 2019) distinguish assignment—directing someone to perform activities within their scope or routine role (for example, assigning an LPN to care for stable clients, or a nursing assistant to give routine hygiene)—from delegation—allowing someone to perform a specific nursing task beyond their usual role after training and competence verification. In both, the RN remains accountable. What the RN never delegates to assistive personnel: initial and ongoing assessment that requires nursing judgment, care planning, client teaching, evaluation of outcomes, and care of unstable clients or clients with unpredictable outcomes. LPNs may care for stable clients with predictable outcomes, collect data, reinforce teaching the RN has begun, and administer many medications per state rules, but the RN retains comprehensive assessment, the plan of care, initial teaching, and evaluation.

Use the five rights of delegation to decide and to supervise: the right task (one that can be delegated, is on the delegatee’s permitted list, and is not assessment, teaching, or evaluation), the right circumstance (a stable client with a predictable outcome and adequate resources), the right person (the delegatee has the training and verified competence), the right directions and communication (clear, specific, including what to report and when—“strain every void, save any stone in the specimen cup, and tell me immediately if you see blood clots or he has new pain”), and the right supervision and evaluation (checking in, reviewing results, intervening, and giving feedback).

check.q: An RN has four tasks: (1) teach a newly diagnosed client to self-inject insulin, (2) obtain a fingerstick glucose on a stable client, (3) assess a client who just returned from surgery, (4) ambulate a client who has walked independently since yesterday. Which can be delegated to a nursing assistant?
check.a: Tasks 2 and 4 (if the fingerstick is on the assistant’s approved task list and the assistant is competent), with clear directions about which results to report. Teaching (1) and assessing a fresh postoperative client (3) require RN judgment and stay with the RN.

steps: Step 1 — Is the client stable with a predictable outcome? If the client is new, unstable, or changing, keep the client (or that part of the care) with the RN.

Step 2 — Does the activity require assessment, care planning, initial teaching, evaluation, or nursing judgment? If yes, it stays with the RN. An LPN may collect data and reinforce teaching; a UAP may measure and report.

Step 3 — Is the activity within this person’s legal scope or approved task list, and does facility policy allow it? (In North Carolina, check the Nurse Aide I or Nurse Aide II task list and the NCBON delegation decision tree.)
Step 4 — Has this person been trained, and is their competence verified for this task? If not, do the task yourself or arrange training first.

Step 5 — Give specific directions: what to do, for whom, by when, what to save, and exactly which findings to report right away (for example, “strain every void, save any stone in the labeled cup, tell me at once about clots or new pain”).
Step 6 — Supervise and evaluate: check in during the shift, review the results yourself, act on abnormal findings, and give feedback. The task moved; your accountability did not.

sections.heading: Medication accountability: range orders and what you answer for
sections.body:
One hour after the 1-mg dose of hydromorphone, Mr. Epworth rates his pain 8/10 with no relief. The order is 1–4 mg IV PRN, and the nurse gives 3 mg. Will the nurse be accountable if this dose fails? The course’s answer: not for the drug’s pharmacologic failure, provided the nurse assessed accurately, gave a dose within the ordered range and allowed by the order’s frequency and facility policy, and monitored the response. The nurse is accountable for reassessing pain and sedation afterward and for notifying the provider if the ordered regimen remains ineffective.

This distinction—you are not accountable for a drug’s biology, you are accountable for your process—is a favorite exam theme. The process includes: verifying the order (including any range-order policy that tells nurses how to titrate within a range), assessing pain, sedation level, respiratory rate and depth, and SpO2 before each dose; considering client factors (a 78-year-old is at higher risk of opioid-induced respiratory depression, so start lower and monitor closely); administering correctly; reassessing at the expected peak time (often about 15–30 minutes for IV opioids); and escalating if relief is inadequate or adverse effects appear. Sedation increases before respiratory depression, so a client who becomes progressively harder to keep awake is a warning sign even when the respiratory rate is still acceptable.

Accountability also includes reporting your own errors. If a nurse gives the wrong dose, the priority is to assess the client and intervene for any harm, then notify the provider, document the facts of the care given in the record (without referring to the event report), and complete an event report per policy.
sections.example: Before giving the 3-mg dose, the nurse notes that Mr. Epworth is alert, respirations 18 and regular, SpO2 96% on room air. Thirty minutes after the dose, he is drowsy but easily aroused, respirations 14, pain 5/10. The nurse documents, keeps monitoring sedation and respirations, offers repositioning, and calls the provider because pain remains moderate and he has now received the higher end of the range—asking whether to add a non-opioid analgesic such as an IV NSAID if not contraindicated (for a 78-year-old, the nurse first checks renal function, bleeding risk, and GI history, because older adults have higher NSAID risk).

check.q: Which part of the hydromorphone situation is the nurse accountable for: the drug’s failure to relieve pain, or the reassessment 30 minutes later?
check.a: The reassessment (and the actions that follow from it). The nurse is accountable for a sound process—assessment, correct dose within the order, monitoring, and escalation—not for an individual client’s pharmacologic response.

sections.heading: Safety, infection, trauma, and suicide screening: matrix duties in action
sections.body:
Safety. The nurse identifies and addresses immediate environmental hazards (spills, clutter, bed not in low position, call light out of reach), assesses the client’s risk for injury outside the healthcare setting, reports safety concerns to supervisors according to unit and institutional policy, and teaches injury-prevention behaviors such as helmet use for cycling and correct child safety restraints. The immediate hazard always comes first: fix it, then report.

Infection. The nurse assesses the client’s history for immunocompromised states (autoimmune disease, cancer, chemotherapy), knows how diseases are transmitted, uses PPE appropriately, and educates the public on immunizations and hygiene. Accountability here includes self-awareness: a nurse with a fever, vomiting, or an unprotected exposure is accountable for reporting it to employee health and following exclusion policy rather than working and transmitting infection to clients.

Trauma and suicide. The nurse assesses for signs of physical, emotional, or sexual abuse; screens for both abuse risk and suicide risk as part of every admission; and stays alert for verbalized or demonstrated warning signs. Screen for abuse privately, away from the person accompanying the client. Ask about suicide directly (“Are you thinking about killing yourself?”)—asking does not plant the idea. When abuse is suspected, the nurse documents objective findings and the client’s own words, ensures safety, and reports to the designated agency as required by law. The duty is to report reasonable suspicion; the nurse does not need proof and does not investigate. Some injuries (for example, gunshot wounds) must be reported according to state statute even when the client asks the nurse not to.
