check.q: During triage, a woman with a facial bruise says she “walked into a door.” Her partner answers every question for her. What should the nurse do first?
check.a: Arrange to interview the client privately (for example, during a procedure or with the partner asked to step out per policy) and ask direct, nonjudgmental abuse-screening questions. Safety planning, documentation of objective findings and her words, resources, and any legally required reporting follow from what the private screen reveals.

sections.heading: Unsafe orders, the chain of command, and owning errors
sections.body:
The ANA Code of Ethics establishes that nurses owe their primary commitment to the client, must protect client health and safety, and are individually accountable for their own judgments and actions. When a physician writes an order that may endanger a client and refuses to change it, the nurse’s ethical obligation is to refuse to carry out the unsafe order, document the communication, and immediately escalate through the facility’s chain of command—charge nurse, nursing supervisor, and medical director or chief nursing officer—to safeguard the client. The nurse should also inform the prescriber that the order is being held.

Escalation is not insubordination; it is accountability. Use assertive, structured communication. TeamSTEPPS offers tools such as CUS (“I am Concerned… I am Uncomfortable… This is a Safety issue”) and the two-challenge rule (voice a concern at least twice; if it is still dismissed, take stronger action and move up the chain). Any team member can “stop the line” for a safety concern. Document objectively in the medical record what was ordered, the client data, who was contacted and when, and what was decided—without editorializing or blaming.

When an error or near miss happens, accountability means transparency. Assess and protect the client first; notify the provider; document the care and the client’s condition factually; complete an event report (a confidential quality-improvement document that is not filed in or mentioned in the chart); and participate in the review. Under Just Culture, the organization consoles a nurse for a human error (a slip or lapse), coaches at-risk behavior (a drift such as skipping a scan because it is slow), and applies discipline for reckless behavior (conscious disregard of a substantial, unjustifiable risk). Reporting is how systems learn; hiding errors is how they repeat.
steps: Assess the client and confirm why the order seems unsafe (data, references, pharmacist input).
Contact the prescriber, state the concern clearly with SBAR or CUS, and request a change.
If the prescriber refuses and the order remains unsafe: do not carry it out; tell the prescriber you are holding it.
Notify the charge nurse immediately; if unresolved, the nursing supervisor/manager; then the medical director or chief nursing officer per policy.
Keep monitoring and protecting the client while the issue is resolved.
Document the facts in the record; complete an event report if policy requires (never mention it in the chart).

check.q: A provider orders a medication dose that the pharmacist and drug reference both confirm is ten times the usual maximum. The provider says, “Just give it, I know what I’m doing.” What does the nurse do next?
check.a: Withhold the dose, tell the provider it will not be given as written, and notify the charge nurse/nursing supervisor immediately to escalate through the chain of command; continue monitoring the client and document the facts. The nurse is accountable for an unsafe action even if it was ordered.

sections.heading: Common traps & look-alikes
sections.body: Use this table when two answers both sound responsible. The difference is usually who owns the decision, whether the client is stable, and whether the action is within scope.

rows: Delegation vs assignment
Delegation = specific nursing task beyond the person’s usual role; assignment = activities within the person’s scope/routine role
Either way the RN stays accountable; the exam usually asks whether the task matches the person and the client’s stability.
Data collection vs assessment
LPN/UAP can collect and report data; the RN interprets and assesses
Words like “evaluate,” “determine,” “interpret,” “assess” mean RN.
Reinforcing teaching vs initial teaching
LPN may reinforce; RN performs initial teaching and evaluates learning
“New diagnosis,” “first time,” or “discharge teaching” = RN.
Stable/predictable vs unstable/unpredictable client
Only stable, predictable clients go to LPNs/UAP
New symptoms, fresh post-op, changing vital signs = keep with RN.
Respecting a refusal vs abandoning the problem
Honor informed refusal, but keep exploring, offering alternatives, and notifying
Correct option continues to act (educate, offer alternatives, notify).
Clarifying an order vs changing it
Nurses clarify with the prescriber; they don’t independently change medical orders
Eliminate options where the nurse adjusts a rate or dose on her own.
Reporting suspicion vs proving abuse
The legal duty is to report reasonable suspicion; investigation belongs to the agency
Eliminate options that wait for proof or confront the suspected abuser.
Event report vs chart documentation
Event report is confidential QI; chart contains only factual care
Eliminate “document in the chart that an incident report was filed.”

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: delegation, unsafe orders, and reporting decisions
sections.body:
Expect four item families. (1) Delegation/assignment: “Which task can the RN delegate to the nursing assistant?” or “Which client should the charge nurse assign to the LPN?” (2) Unsafe or questionable orders: “Which action should the nurse take first?” when an order conflicts with the client’s condition or evidence. (3) Mandatory reporting and screening: suspected child or elder abuse, suicide risk, reportable injuries. (4) Errors and accountability after the fact: who is accountable, what to document, and what to report. In each family the correct answer keeps nursing judgment with the RN, protects the client first, and uses legitimate channels.

Walk through this original sample item.
steps: Read the stem: “An RN is working with an LPN and a nursing assistant on a medical unit. Which client is most appropriate for the RN to assign to the LPN?” (A) A client admitted 30 minutes ago with chest pain awaiting the first troponin result. (B) A client with a stable chronic leg ulcer who needs a scheduled dressing change and routine oral medications. (C) A client who requires initial teaching on a new home tube feeding regimen. (D) A client 2 hours after a thyroidectomy reporting new tingling around the mouth.
Identify what is being asked: matching the LPN’s scope to the client who is stable with a predictable outcome.
Spot cues: “admitted 30 minutes ago,” “initial teaching,” and “new tingling” all signal RN-level work; “stable chronic” and “routine” signal predictability.
Eliminate (A): a new admission with possible acute coronary syndrome is unstable and needs RN assessment.
Eliminate (C): initial teaching is an RN accountability; the LPN could reinforce it later.
Eliminate (D): circumoral tingling after thyroidectomy suggests hypocalcemia—an acute change requiring RN assessment and prompt action.
Choose (B): a stable client with routine, predictable care falls within LPN scope.

Reusable strategy: sort options into stable/predictable vs new/changing/teaching/assessment. Assign the stable, routine client to the LPN or UAP; keep anything new, unstable, or requiring judgment with the RN.

sections.heading: Worked case: a night shift with a missed specimen, a fluid order, and a bruise
sections.body: Dana, an RN on a medical-surgical night shift, has five clients and works with an LPN, Rob, and a nursing assistant, Kia. At 2200 she receives handoff. Mr. Ortiz, 81, with heart failure, has a new order for 0.9% saline at 250 mL/hr for “dehydration”; his lungs had fine crackles at the bases on the evening assessment. Ms. Patel, 30, admitted for renal colic, has an order to strain all urine; Rob is assigned to her. Mrs. Greene, 84, admitted from home with a hip fracture, has bruises in different stages of healing on both upper arms; her adult son, who lives with her, answers every question and refuses to leave the room.
steps: Recognize cues: (1) a high fluid rate in an older client with heart failure and crackles; (2) a straining order that requires clear communication to the LPN; (3) patterned bruising of different ages in a dependent older adult with a controlling caregiver.

Prioritize: Mr. Ortiz has a potential physiologic threat (fluid overload). Dana assesses him first—respiratory rate, SpO2, lung sounds, edema, weight, intake and output—before or as the fluid infuses.

Take action on the order: Dana contacts the provider with SBAR: “Mr. Ortiz is 81 with heart failure; he has bibasilar crackles and SpO2 93%. NS is ordered at 250 mL/hr. I recommend a lower rate or reevaluation.” If the provider maintained an unsafe order, she would hold it and escalate through the charge nurse and supervisor.

Delegate/assign accurately: Dana confirms with Rob that Ms. Patel’s urine must be strained every void, that any stone is saved in a labeled cup, and that new severe pain, fever, or inability to void is reported immediately. She asks Kia to measure and report Mr. Ortiz’s urine output every 2 hours and to tell her right away if he has trouble breathing.

Address suspected abuse: Dana finds a moment to speak with Mrs. Greene privately (when the son steps out or by asking him to wait outside per policy for the assessment), asks direct screening questions, documents the bruises objectively (location, size, color, pattern) and Mrs. Greene’s own words, notifies the provider and charge nurse, and makes a report to adult protective services according to state law and policy (in North Carolina, a report to the county department of social services under G.S. 108A-102 when a disabled adult may need protective services). She does not confront the son or wait for proof.
Evaluate: at 2400 Dana rechecks Mr. Ortiz’s respiratory status on the revised rate, reviews Ms. Patel’s strained specimens with Rob, and follows up on the abuse report and the social work referral.

check.q: At 0300, Rob tells Dana he forgot to strain one void. Who is accountable, and what should Dana do?
check.a: Rob is accountable for his performance, and Dana remains accountable for supervision and the client outcome. Dana reinforces the instruction, considers whether more supervision is needed, notifies the provider if the missed specimen matters to the plan, documents factually, and completes an event report if policy requires. She gives Rob feedback without blame, consistent with Just Culture (a human error).

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
Delegation and assignment. Under the NCBON rules (21 NCAC 36 .0224 for RNs; .0225 for LPNs), the RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment; the LPN participates under the supervision of an RN or other authorized provider. The RN may delegate tasks, not the nursing process or nursing judgment. NCBON publishes a Decision Tree for Delegation to UAP. North Carolina has two nurse aide levels: Nurse Aide I (registry kept by the NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation) and Nurse Aide II (registry kept by NCBON; must also be listed on the NA I registry). NA II tasks include some sterile and more advanced tasks—such as sterile dressing changes and oxygen therapy—per the NCBON NA II task list. A task must be on the aide’s approved list and the RN must decide that delegation is appropriate for this specific client.

Mandatory reporting. North Carolina is a universal reporting state for children. Under G.S. 7B-301, any person or institution with cause to suspect that a juvenile (under 18) is abused, neglected, or dependent, or has died from maltreatment, must report to the county department of social services (DSS) director. Knowingly failing to report is a crime. Report suspicion; do not investigate or wait for proof. Good-faith reporters are immune. For adults, G.S. 108A-102 requires any person with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult is in need of protective services to report to the county DSS director, orally or in writing; good-faith reporters are immune.

Practice events and conduct. NCBON uses a Just Culture–based Complaint Evaluation Tool that classifies practice events as human error, at-risk behavior, or reckless behavior. Conduct issues—drug diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary or sexual misconduct, and confidentiality breaches—are reported to the Board, not handled only by the employer. NCBON offers alternative-to-discipline programs for nurses with substance use disorders.
bullets: A task on the NA II list is not automatically appropriate for every client—the RN still applies the delegation decision tree to the client in front of her.
In NC, a hospital’s internal child-abuse process does not replace the individual’s legal duty to ensure a report reaches county DSS.
Older adults are covered by G.S. 108A-102 when they meet the definition of a disabled adult needing protective services; report reasonable suspicion to county DSS.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Source: Module 42 study guide, “Expanded Duties Under Accountability” (p. 2704), “Concepts Related to Accountability & Nursing Implications Matrix” (p. 2705), Case Study Part 1: Ms. Kathryn Miller (p. 2704), Case Study 2: Mr. Frank Epworth (p. 2710), and Review & Relate “Linking Accountability to Ethics” (p. 2710). Added national content: NCSBN/ANA (2019) delegation and assignment guidelines, the five rights of delegation, TeamSTEPPS CUS and two-challenge rule, SBAR, Just Culture, and event-report documentation rules.
bullets: Delegation vs assignment: the Epworth case says the RN “delegates” urine straining to an LPN. Under the 2019 NCSBN/ANA guidelines, directing an LPN to perform work within the LPN’s scope is usually called an assignment. The conclusion is the same: the RN retains accountability for communication, supervision, and evaluation.

Comfort assessment frequency: the matrix says “at least once per shift.” That is a minimum. Pain is also assessed on admission, with each new report or change, and reassessed after every intervention at the expected peak effect (commonly about 15–30 minutes after IV and 30–60 minutes after oral analgesics), per facility policy.

Hydromorphone redosing: giving 3 mg one hour after 1 mg is acceptable only if the order’s frequency and the facility’s range-order policy allow it; in a 78-year-old, monitor sedation level and respirations closely because sedation precedes respiratory depression.

Mandatory reporting: the course says nurses report abuse of “children and older adults.” Requirements vary by state; in North Carolina, adult reporting applies to disabled adults in need of protective services (G.S. 108A-102), and child reporting is universal (G.S. 7B-301).
Unsafe-order refusal: the course says to refuse an unsafe order. Also tell the prescriber you are holding it and keep monitoring the client while the chain of command resolves the issue.

mnemonics.name: Five rights of delegation: “Tasks Can Pass Down Safely”
What the RN keeps: “EAT” (never delegated to UAP)
mnemonics.text: Evaluate • Assess • Teach—plus care of anyone unstable or unpredictable.

mnemonics.name: TeamSTEPPS CUS
mnemonics.text: I’m Concerned • I’m Uncomfortable • This is a Safety issue—say it, then escalate if the concern is dismissed (two-challenge rule).

pearls: “I delegated it” is never a complete answer: the RN stays accountable for the decision, the directions, the supervision, and the follow-up.
When words and cues conflict (“I’m fine” with guarding and elevated BP), believe the full picture and complete the assessment.
Respecting a refusal means documenting it and continuing to educate, offer alternatives, and notify—not dropping the problem.
Clarify any order that conflicts with evidence or the client’s condition before implementing; never change it on your own.
You are accountable for your process (assessment, correct dose, monitoring, escalation), not for an individual client’s pharmacologic response.
Screen every client for abuse and suicide risk at admission; screen for abuse privately and ask about suicide directly.
Report suspicion of abuse or neglect—you do not need proof, and you do not investigate.
Event reports are confidential QI documents; chart only the facts of the client’s care.
redFlags: A client with heart failure, older age, or renal disease receiving a high IV fluid rate: assess for overload and clarify the order.
Increasing sedation after an opioid—even with a normal respiratory rate—is a warning sign of impending respiratory depression.
Injuries inconsistent with the history, injuries in different stages of healing, or a caregiver who will not let the client speak alone suggest abuse.
A client who says others would be “better off without me” needs an immediate direct suicide assessment and a safe environment.
Delegating to a UAP the care of a client whose status is changing puts the client at risk and violates delegation principles.
recap: Accountability governs holistic wellness, physical outcomes, safety, trauma/abuse/suicide, education, and infection prevention.
The related-concepts matrix pairs each concept with concrete actions: assess, intervene, report, teach, refer, document.
Complete the assessment before leaving the room; incongruent cues demand follow-up and collaboration.
EBP accountability means bringing current evidence to the prescriber or practice council—not ignoring the concern or changing orders yourself.
The RN stays accountable after assigning or delegating; apply the five rights and never delegate assessment, teaching, evaluation, or unstable clients to UAP.
Unsafe order + prescriber refusal → do not carry it out, inform the prescriber, escalate through the chain of command, document facts.
Report suspected abuse to the designated agency without waiting for proof; screen every client for abuse and suicide risk.
Errors and near misses are disclosed and reported; Just Culture consoles human error, coaches at-risk behavior, and sanctions reckless behavior.

checks.q: A nursing assistant reports that a client’s blood pressure is 182/104 and the client has a new headache. The RN is in the middle of a dressing change on another client. What is the best action?
checks.a: Arrange to see the hypertensive client promptly (ask another nurse to complete or cover the dressing change if it cannot be paused safely), assess the client personally, and notify the provider. The assistant cannot interpret or act on the finding; a new symptom with severe hypertension is RN work.

checks.q: Which instruction to an LPN best meets the “right directions and communication” standard for straining urine: “Keep an eye on his urine,” or “Strain every void, save anything you catch in the labeled cup, and tell me right away about clots or new pain”?
checks.a: The second. Directions must be specific about what to do, what to save, and what and when to report.

checks.q: A provider orders morphine for a client whose respiratory rate is 8 and who is difficult to arouse. The provider insists on giving it. List the nurse’s sequence.
checks.a: Hold the dose and protect the client (stimulate, support breathing, follow the opioid-reversal protocol/rapid response as indicated), tell the provider the dose is being held, escalate to the charge nurse/supervisor, and document the facts.

checks.q: A 15-year-old in the emergency department has a spiral fracture of the humerus; the parent says the child “fell off the couch.” Is the nurse required to have proof before reporting?
checks.a: No. The nurse reports reasonable suspicion of abuse to the designated child protective agency (in NC, county DSS) and documents objectively. Investigation is the agency’s role.

checks.q: A nurse forgot to check a client’s blood glucose before giving scheduled insulin; the client is now diaphoretic and shaky. What comes first: the event report or the client?
checks.a: The client. Check glucose and treat hypoglycemia per protocol, notify the provider, document the care, and then complete the event report per policy.

checks.q: An NA II in North Carolina is approved to perform sterile dressing changes. A client’s wound has new purulent drainage and the client has a fever. Should the RN delegate today’s dressing change to the NA II?
checks.a: No. The task is on the NA II list, but this client’s situation has changed and requires RN assessment of the wound. The task must be permitted AND appropriate for the specific client at that time.

topics.title: Exemplar 42.A Competence: Critical Thinking, Emotional Intelligence, Benner’s Stages & Practicing Within Your Limits
topics.summary: Competence is practicing nursing to the fullest extent with specialized knowledge, skills, abilities, and clinical judgment; it rests on critical thinking, problem solving (supported by emotional intelligence), and ethical reasoning, grows through Benner’s five stages, and always includes knowing your limits and asking for help.
objectives: Analyze how competence relates to accountability and why a nurse cannot be accountable for care he or she is not competent to give.
Describe the three core areas of competence—critical thinking, problem solving, and ethical reasoning/decision making—and recognize each in clinical behavior.
Explain emotional intelligence (EI) and identify when emotions rather than objective data are driving a clinical decision.
Compare Benner’s five stages (novice to expert) and apply them to describe a nurse’s performance.
Apply the first rule of competence—ask for help whenever there is uncertainty about safety—including double-checking high-risk actions at every level of expertise.
Respond appropriately when asked to float or accept an assignment beyond one’s competence.
Identify the core elements of cultural competence and strategies for maintaining lifelong competence.
topics.bigPicture:
Competence is the bridge between knowing and doing. A competent nurse uses specialized knowledge, skills, abilities, and clinical judgment to give safe care—and also knows the edges of that knowledge. The course defines competence to include “awareness of personal capabilities and limitations” and openness to feedback and change. That last part surprises students: the most competent nurse in the room is not the one who never asks questions, but the one who knows exactly when to ask.

Competence is inseparable from accountability. You can be held accountable only for care you are prepared to give, so accepting work you are not competent to do is itself an accountability failure—toward the client, toward your license, and toward the colleagues who trust you. That is why the floating case in this exemplar (an experienced labor-and-delivery nurse asked to take a NICU assignment) is a classic exam scenario: the right answer is neither blind compliance nor walking off the unit, but honest communication about competence and negotiation of a safe role.

On the NCLEX, competence appears in questions about floating and assignments, about new graduates and preceptors, about a nurse’s own fatigue or impairment, about double-checking high-alert medications, about recognizing when emotion is clouding judgment, and about culturally responsive care. The thread is consistent: safety requires honesty about what you know and what you do not.

keyTerms.def: Practicing nursing to the fullest extent by using specialized knowledge, skills, abilities, and clinical judgment when enacting client care; the competent nurse applies critical thinking, problem solving, and ethical reasoning, is aware of personal capabilities and limitations, and remains open to feedback and change.

Purposeful, reflective reasoning that begins in nursing school and deepens at the bedside; critical thinkers stay open to others’ opinions while relying on evidence, recognize their limits, and inquire and investigate before acting.
Applying classroom theory to diverse, real-world clinical contexts so that knowledge becomes usable judgment.
Identifying a clinical problem and working through it to a solution in complex environments; developed over time through EBP and practice and dependent on self-awareness and emotional intelligence.

A nurse’s ability to recognize, through emotional appraisal, when personal emotions rather than objective knowledge are influencing clinical decisions; it strengthens relationships with clients and interprofessional peers and is essential to self-awareness in problem solving.

Applying ethical principles and the ANA Code of Ethics to everyday practice decisions in every setting, respecting client preferences and circumstances, and monitoring one’s own physical and emotional fitness to practice.
No experience (e.g., a nursing student); limited, inflexible performance governed by context-free rules and regulations rather than experience.
New graduate or early clinical exposure; marginally acceptable performance; recognizes meaningful recurring aspects of real situations based on prior experience.
About 2–3 years of experience in the same or similar setting; strong organization and planning; separates important factors from less important ones; coordinates multiple complex care demands.
About 3–5 years of experience; perceives situations as wholes rather than parts; uses maxims as guides; holistic understanding improves decision making; focuses on long-term goals.

Extensive experience; fluid, flexible, highly proficient performance that no longer relies on rules, guidelines, or maxims to connect understanding to action; uses highly skilled intuitive and analytic ability (“it felt right”).
Always ask for help whenever there is any uncertainty about the safety of an action; saying “I don’t know” or “Would you help me?” is safer and more honorable than guessing.

The ability to provide care that respects and responds to clients’ cultural values, beliefs, and practices—built through self-awareness of one’s own values, strong listening, understanding cultural rites and traditions, advocacy, and use of community resources.
Temporarily reassigning a nurse to a unit other than the home unit to meet staffing needs; the nurse must accept only those responsibilities within his or her competence.

Preventable differences in health outcomes among groups; the IOM report Unequal Treatment (2002) linked them in part to providers’ lack of cultural understanding, language barriers, low education, limited social support, lack of insurance, poor housing, and discriminatory attitudes.

sections.heading: What competence is—and why it is the partner of accountability
sections.body:
The exemplar has three learning outcomes: analyze competence as it relates to accountability, describe the areas of competence, and explain why lifelong competence matters. Start with the relationship. Accountability says “I answer for my care.” Competence says “I am capable of giving that care safely.” A nurse who is accountable but not competent is a danger; a nurse who is competent but not accountable is unreliable. The profession requires both.

Competence is not a credential you earn once. It is a moving target that changes with each new unit, technology, population, and guideline. A nurse can be expert in labor and delivery and a novice in the NICU on the same day. Competence is also self-aware: it includes knowing personal capabilities and limits and staying open to feedback and change. That is why the course places “awareness of limitations” inside the definition rather than treating it as a separate virtue.

Competence reassures the public. Clients trust nurses because they assume the person caring for them is prepared. Preserving that trust requires a supportive unit culture that encourages questioning, team collaboration, error reporting, and lifelong education. A unit where nurses are afraid to say “I have never done this” is a unit where competence is being faked—and where harm is more likely.
sections.analogy: Competence is like a driver’s skill in a specific vehicle and road. A safe commuter car driver is not automatically safe driving a loaded semi-truck on an icy mountain pass. Being a good driver includes recognizing when a vehicle or road exceeds your experience—and asking for a co-driver or a different route rather than “figuring it out as you go.”

check.q: A nurse with 12 years of adult ICU experience is assigned a pediatric oncology client for the first time and says, “I’m an ICU nurse; I can handle anything.” Which element of competence is missing?
check.a: Awareness of personal capabilities and limitations (and openness to help). Years of expertise in one area do not transfer automatically to a different population; the nurse should acknowledge the gap and seek resources, orientation, or a mentor.

sections.heading: Core area 1: critical thinking and situational learning
sections.body:
Critical thinking begins in nursing school and deepens at the bedside through situational learning—applying classroom theory to diverse real-world situations. In school you learn that a falling blood pressure and rising heart rate can signal hypovolemia; at the bedside you learn what that looks like in a 90-year-old on a beta-blocker whose heart rate cannot rise. Theory becomes judgment through repeated, reflective application.

The course describes critical thinkers by their behaviors: they remain open to others’ opinions while relying on evidence, recognize personal limits, and inquire and investigate before acting. Each behavior has an exam translation. “Open to others while relying on evidence” means you listen to a family member who says “this isn’t like him,” and you verify with assessment data. “Recognize limits” means you call for help when the situation exceeds your preparation. “Inquire and investigate before acting” is the NCLEX’s favorite rule: assess before you act, unless the situation is an emergency where immediate action is the assessment-guided response.

Critical thinking is also the opposite of task completion. A nurse who gives the scheduled antihypertensive because “it’s 0900” without checking the blood pressure of 88/52 is completing a task; the critical thinker asks whether the action still makes sense for this client right now.
sections.example: A family member says, “Mom is never this confused—something is wrong.” The client is oriented to name only; her chart lists “baseline dementia.” A nurse thinking critically does not dismiss the family (“she has dementia”) or panic; she investigates: checks vital signs, SpO2, glucose, recent medications, signs of infection, and compares with the documented baseline—then reports the acute change.

check.q: Which nurse is demonstrating critical thinking: one who documents a new irregular pulse and plans to mention it at handoff, or one who obtains an apical pulse and rhythm strip, checks the client for symptoms, and notifies the provider of the new finding?
check.a: The second. Critical thinking means investigating a new cue and acting on it promptly, not deferring it.

sections.heading: Core area 2: problem solving and emotional intelligence
sections.body:
Problem solving is essential in complex environments where several issues compete and information is incomplete. It develops over time through EBP and clinical practice. The course adds a crucial condition: problem solving requires self-awareness and emotional intelligence so that emotions do not override objective clinical judgment.

Emotional intelligence is the nurse’s ability to recognize, through emotional appraisal, when personal emotions rather than objective knowledge are shaping a decision. Emotions are not the enemy—empathy, concern, and even a gut sense of unease are clinically useful—but they become dangerous when they replace data. Common examples: a nurse who dislikes a demanding client delays answering that client’s call light; a nurse who feels intimidated by a physician avoids calling about a worrisome finding; a nurse who is frustrated with a client who “always says 10/10 pain” stops assessing that client’s pain objectively; a nurse who identifies with a young client minimizes signs of withdrawal because “he seems like a good kid.”

EI also strengthens working relationships with clients and interprofessional peers. A nurse who can notice “I am angry right now” can pause, regulate, and respond professionally—choosing therapeutic communication instead of reacting. On the exam, EI items often ask which action shows self-awareness: the correct option names the emotion, separates it from the data, and refocuses on objective assessment or seeks a colleague’s perspective.

rows: “He’s just drug-seeking.”
Frustration is replacing assessment
Assess pain with a scale and objective signs; treat per order; involve the team in a pain plan
“I don’t want to bother Dr. X again.”
Fear of conflict is delaying escalation
Use SBAR and call with the data; escalate if needed
“She reminds me of my grandmother; she can’t be getting worse.”
Attachment is filtering out cues
Compare vital signs and assessment with baseline; report changes
“That family is so rude—I’ll check on them later.”
Irritation is affecting priority setting
Prioritize by client need, not by personal comfort

check.q: A nurse realizes she has avoided entering the room of a verbally hostile client for two hours. Which action demonstrates emotional intelligence?
check.a: Acknowledge to herself that her discomfort is driving the delay, go assess the client now (with a colleague or security per policy if safety is a concern), and discuss strategies with the charge nurse. Avoidance based on emotion is a safety risk.

sections.heading: Core area 3: ethical reasoning, decision making, and fitness for duty
sections.body:
Ethical reasoning and decision making are grounded in the ANA Code of Ethics and are needed in every practice setting, not just critical care. Ethics is not only end-of-life debates; it is deciding whether to tell a client the truth about a delay, whether to respect a refusal, how to divide limited time fairly among clients, and whether to speak up about a colleague’s unsafe shortcut. The principles you will use include autonomy (respecting the client’s right to decide), beneficence (doing good), nonmaleficence (avoiding harm), justice (fairness), fidelity (keeping promises), and veracity (truthfulness).

Ethical competence requires the nurse to respect client preferences and circumstances. A competent nurse does not impose her own values on a client’s informed decision; she makes sure the decision is informed and supported. It also requires the nurse to monitor her own physical and emotional well-being, because working while compromised—exhausted, ill, impaired by substances or medications, or emotionally overwhelmed—endangers clients. Fitness for duty is part of competence.

This is where competence links to accountability most directly: a nurse who comes to work after a double shift and no sleep, or who takes a sedating medication before a shift, may be technically skilled but is not competent to practice safely at that moment. The accountable choice is to tell the supervisor, decline additional hours, or seek help—before an error occurs.
sections.example: A nurse is asked to stay for a second consecutive 12-hour shift. She has been awake for 20 hours and nearly scanned the wrong client’s wristband an hour ago. Ethically and competently, she tells the supervisor she is too fatigued to practice safely, offers to help find coverage or stay briefly for a safe handoff, and declines the extra shift.

check.q: Is ethical reasoning a competence only for nurses in ICUs, hospice, or ethics committees?
check.a: No. The course emphasizes that ethical reasoning is needed across all everyday practice settings—for example, truth-telling, respecting refusals, fair prioritization, and reporting unsafe practice.

sections.heading: Benner’s five stages: how experience becomes expertise
sections.body:
Patricia Benner’s model (From Novice to Expert) describes how clinical experience builds expertise in five stages. The key idea is that nurses move from relying on rules to relying on experience-based perception. A novice needs explicit rules because she has no experience to tell her what matters; an expert perceives the situation as a whole and responds fluidly, often before she can explain why.

Stages are specific to a setting. A nurse who is an expert on a cardiac step-down unit may be an advanced beginner after transferring to pediatrics. That is why orientation, preceptors, and competency validation are required whenever a nurse changes specialty, and why a float nurse should not be given the same independent assignment as a nurse who works on that unit every day.

Benner’s model also explains common exam distractors. The advanced beginner “recognizes meaningful recurring aspects” but still needs help setting priorities in complex situations—so a preceptor should help a new graduate prioritize, not leave her alone with the most unstable client. The competent nurse (2–3 years) organizes and plans well and can coordinate complex demands. The proficient nurse (3–5 years) sees the whole picture and uses maxims (“a client who suddenly says ‘something is wrong’ needs to be seen now”). The expert uses intuition—but, as the safety alert reminds us, still double-checks high-risk actions.

headers: What it looks like at the bedside
rows: I. Novice
No experience (nursing student)
Context-free rules and regulations; limited and inflexible
Follows the checklist exactly; struggles when the situation differs from the textbook
II. Advanced beginner
New graduate / early clinical exposure
Recognizes recurring meaningful aspects from prior experience; marginally acceptable performance
Notices “this looks like last week’s client” but needs help prioritizing several needs
III. Competent
About 2–3 years
Conscious, deliberate planning; separates important from less important factors
Organizes the day well; coordinates multiple complex demands
IV. Proficient
About 3–5 years
Perceives situations as wholes; uses maxims; focuses on long-term goals
Anticipates the discharge plan and spots a subtle deterioration pattern
V. Expert
Extensive experience
Intuitive and analytic; no longer needs rules or maxims to link understanding to action
“It felt right”—acts fluidly; still double-checks high-alert actions

check.q: A nurse with 4 years on the same oncology unit says, “When a neutropenic client starts acting even a little ‘off,’ I treat it as sepsis until proven otherwise,” and plans ahead for the client’s discharge needs. Which Benner stage best fits?
check.a: Proficient (about 3–5 years): she perceives situations as wholes, uses a maxim to guide action, and focuses on long-term goals.

steps: Step 1 — Check the setting first. Years count only in the same or a similar setting; an experienced nurse who has just changed specialty may be a novice or advanced beginner there.
Step 2 — Look for how the nurse decides. Following context-free rules or checklists with no experience → novice. Recognizing recurring aspects but needing help to prioritize → advanced beginner.
Step 3 — Organization and deliberate planning that sorts important from less important factors and coordinates several complex demands → competent (about 2–3 years).
Step 4 — Seeing the situation as a whole, using maxims (“if X, then see the client now”), and focusing on long-term goals such as discharge → proficient (about 3–5 years).
Step 5 — Fluid, intuitive action that no longer needs rules or maxims (“something isn’t right”), with analysis used when something is unfamiliar → expert.
Step 6 — Apply the safety alert at every stage: any option in which a nurse, even an expert, skips a double-check or refuses to ask for help is wrong.

sections.heading: The safety alert: double-check, say “I don’t know,” and ask for help
sections.body:
The course’s safety alert carries three rules that apply at every level of expertise. Expert vigilance: even expert nurses continue to double-check high-risk actions such as medication doses and sterilization. Expertise reduces some errors but creates others—speed, habit, and confidence can let a misplaced decimal point slip through. Independent double-checks for high-alert medications (insulin infusions, heparin, chemotherapy, pediatric weight-based doses, PCA programming) are a system safeguard, not an insult to skill.

Honesty and humility over guessing: regardless of proficiency, it is always more honorable and safer to say “I don’t know” or “Would you help me?” than to say “I’m not sure, but I think this is right” or “I’ll figure it out as I go along.” The first rule of competence: always ask for help whenever there is any uncertainty about the safety of an action.

On the NCLEX, this principle often appears in the form of a nurse’s statement. Statements that admit uncertainty and seek help or verification (“I haven’t used this pump before—can you check my programming?”) are correct. Statements that guess, rationalize, or postpone checking (“I’m pretty sure it’s the same as the old pump”) indicate a need for further teaching.

rows: “I’m not sure, but I think this dose is right.”
“This dose looks unusual to me—I’m going to verify it with the pharmacist before I give it.”
“I’ll figure the new pump out as I go along.”
“I haven’t been trained on this pump. Would you help me program it and check my settings?”
“I’ve done this a hundred times; I don’t need a second check.”
“It’s a high-alert drug, so let’s do an independent double-check.”
“I don’t want to look incompetent by asking.”
“I don’t know how to do this safely yet. Who can walk me through it?”

check.q: An expert nurse with 20 years of experience is preparing a heparin infusion. She tells the new graduate, “You don’t need to double-check me—I could do this in my sleep.” How should the new graduate respond?
check.a: Respectfully insist on the independent double-check required by policy for high-alert medications. The safety alert states that experts must still double-check high-risk actions; expertise does not remove the need.

sections.heading: Floating and assignments beyond your competence: the Tyree Campbell case
sections.body:
Tyree Campbell, an L&D RN with 8 years of experience, is asked to float to the NICU because L&D census is low. She panics: she has no NICU experience. Her responsibility is to self-assess her competence, refuse to perform tasks or accept an assignment for which she lacks specialized knowledge and skills, and immediately communicate her limitations to the nursing supervisor to protect neonatal safety. Can she accept an independent NICU assignment? No—doing so would violate professional standards of competence, the ANA Code of Ethics, and the Nurse Practice Act’s safety mandates, placing critically ill neonates at high risk. She may, if mutually agreed, float to perform basic, nonspecialized supportive tasks within her existing competence.

What should she say? Respectfully, clearly, and assertively: “I want to help with staffing, but I have never worked in the NICU and do not have the training or competence to safely care for critically ill neonates. To protect the babies, I can’t accept a full NICU assignment. I’m happy to help with basic tasks within my competence, work alongside a NICU nurse, or float to postpartum or mother-baby, where I am competent.” Notice the structure: willingness to help, a specific statement of the competence gap, the safety reason, and alternatives.

Two important nuances. First, raise concerns before accepting the assignment and receiving report. Once a nurse has accepted responsibility for clients, leaving without a proper handoff can constitute client abandonment. Second, refusing is not the same as walking away from the institution’s need: the accountable nurse negotiates—a buddy assignment, a modified role, an alternative unit—and follows the facility’s process for documenting assignment concerns. Legally, accepting an assignment beyond one’s skill level exposes the nurse to malpractice liability and board discipline; ethically, the nurse has a duty to disclose limitations honestly.
steps: Self-assess: compare the assignment’s demands with your education, orientation, validated competencies, and experience.
Communicate early: tell the supervisor/charge nurse before accepting report, naming the specific gap.
State the safety reason and your willingness to help.
Negotiate options: tasks within competence, a buddy/resource role, reassignment to a unit where you are competent, or orientation.
If the supervisor insists on an unsafe assignment, follow the facility’s chain of command and assignment-objection process; document factually.
Once you accept clients, do not leave them without a proper handoff to another qualified nurse.

check.q: Ms. Campbell is told, “Just take the two most stable babies—you’ll be fine.” Is that an acceptable compromise?
check.a: Not as an independent assignment. Even “stable” NICU neonates require specialized assessment and skills she lacks. An acceptable compromise is a supportive role working with a NICU nurse who retains responsibility for the neonates, performing only tasks within her competence, or reassignment to an area where she is competent.

sections.heading: Cultural competence and lifelong competence
sections.body:
As minority and ethnic populations grow to make up the majority of the U.S. population, nurses must deliver culturally responsive care. The IOM’s 2002 report Unequal Treatment documented health disparities linked to providers’ lack of cultural understanding, along with language barriers, low education, limited social support, lack of insurance, poor housing, and discriminatory attitudes among healthcare providers. Cultural competence is therefore part of competence—not an optional extra.

The course lists four core elements of cultural competence training: (1) recognizing one’s own values and beliefs and how they affect care; (2) developing strong listening skills and understanding cultural rites and traditions; (3) advocating for clients’ wishes when treatments conflict with cultural values, especially in end-of-life or psychiatric care; and (4) identifying community resources for follow-up care to prevent recurrence or readmission. In practice this means asking rather than assuming (“What is important to you and your family about this decision?”), using a qualified medical interpreter rather than family members, and avoiding stereotypes—knowledge about a cultural group is a starting point for questions, not a prediction about an individual. Many educators add cultural humility: lifelong self-reflection and treating the client as the expert on their own culture.

Lifelong competence grows through formal education, seminars, peer-reviewed journals, employer classes, certification, and interprofessional collaboration. When a nurse lacks competence in a specific area, the course lists the remedies: continuing education, workshops, peer-reviewed literature, mentorship or preceptorship, and supervised clinical orientation. Ethically, nurses must maintain ongoing competence, disclose skill limitations honestly, report errors transparently, and engage in lifelong learning so the public receives safe, high-quality care.
bullets: Use a trained medical interpreter (in person, video, or phone) for health information; do not rely on children or family members.
Ask about practices, foods, modesty needs, decision-makers, and spiritual needs instead of assuming.
Advocate when a recommended treatment conflicts with the client’s values—make sure the team knows the client’s wishes and explores acceptable alternatives.
Connect clients to culturally and linguistically appropriate community resources before discharge.

check.q: A client who speaks limited English is being prepared for surgery, and her 12-year-old son offers to interpret. What is the competent action?
check.a: Thank the son and obtain a qualified medical interpreter. Using a child or family member risks inaccurate interpretation, breaches privacy, and places an inappropriate burden on the child.

sections.heading: Common traps & look-alikes
sections.body: Competence items reward precise reading. These are the most common confusions.

rows: Benner’s “competent” stage vs “competence” the concept
The stage is level III (about 2–3 years); the concept applies to all nurses at every stage
If the stem gives years or behaviors, it is asking about the stage.
Competent (III) vs proficient (IV)
Competent = deliberate planning and organization; proficient = sees the whole, uses maxims, long-term goals
“Organizes and prioritizes” vs “perceives as a whole / anticipates”.
Advanced beginner (II) vs novice (I)
Novice uses context-free rules with no experience; advanced beginner recognizes recurring aspects from some experience
Student = novice; new graduate = advanced beginner.
Expert intuition vs skipping safety checks
Experts use intuition but still double-check high-risk actions
Any option where an expert skips a double-check is wrong.
Declining an unsafe assignment vs abandonment
Declining/negotiating before accepting is appropriate; leaving accepted clients without handoff is abandonment
Look for timing: before report vs after accepting the clients.
Critical thinking vs problem solving
Critical thinking = inquiry, openness, evidence, recognizing limits; problem solving = working through a specific clinical problem, supported by EI
“Investigates before acting” = critical thinking; “emotions overriding judgment” = EI/problem solving.
Emotional intelligence vs empathy
Empathy is feeling with the client; EI is noticing when your own emotions are steering decisions
“Recognizes that frustration is affecting care” = EI.
Cultural competence vs stereotyping
Competence asks the individual; stereotyping assumes from group membership
Eliminate options that assume a client’s preferences from ethnicity or religion.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: competence, floating, and the honest “I don’t know”
sections.body:
Competence items usually take one of these shapes: a nurse is asked to float or take an assignment outside her experience; a new graduate or student makes a statement and you must decide whether it shows understanding or needs further teaching; a nurse’s emotions, fatigue, or impairment threaten safety; or a description of a nurse’s behavior asks which Benner stage it reflects. The correct answers share a pattern: honest self-assessment, early communication, seeking help or verification, and keeping the client safe within one’s competence.

Walk through this original item.
steps: Read the stem: “A medical-surgical RN is floated to a pediatric unit and assigned a 4-year-old receiving a continuous IV infusion through a type of smart pump the nurse has never used. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?” (A) Read the pump manual during the shift and program the next bag when it is due. (B) Tell the charge nurse she has not been trained on this pump and ask for help or validation before managing the infusion. (C) Ask the child’s parent to show her how the pump works. (D) Decline the entire assignment and return to her home unit.
Identify what is being asked: the most appropriate response to a specific competence gap during a float assignment.
Spot cues: “never used” (a known gap), a pediatric continuous infusion (high risk of dosing error), and “most appropriate.”
Eliminate (A): this is “I’ll figure it out as I go along”—the unsafe statement the safety alert warns against.
Eliminate (C): the parent is not responsible for verifying device safety; this shifts accountability inappropriately.
Eliminate (D): the gap is a single device, not the whole assignment; leaving without negotiating ignores staffing needs and, if she has already accepted the clients, risks abandonment.
Choose (B): it applies the first rule of competence—acknowledge the limit, communicate it to the right person, and get help or validation before acting.

Reusable strategy: when a stem reveals a gap in knowledge or skill, pick the option that names the gap to the appropriate person and obtains help, training, or reassignment for that specific task; reject guessing, self-teaching on the fly, shifting responsibility to the client/family, and total refusal when a narrower solution exists.

sections.heading: Worked case: the new graduate, the experienced preceptor, and a tense evening
sections.body: Aisha is a new graduate RN in week 8 of orientation on a telemetry unit, precepted by Lou, who has 15 years of experience. Tonight Aisha has four clients. One, Mr. Burke, has been demanding all evening and called her “useless.” At 1900 his telemetry shows a new rhythm Aisha thinks might be atrial fibrillation, and he says he feels “fluttery.” Aisha notices she is reluctant to go back in. Meanwhile, the charge nurse asks whether Aisha can take a fifth client—a fresh admission on a heparin infusion—because the unit is short. Lou says, “You’ll be fine; I barely ever double-check heparin anymore.”
steps: Recognize cues: a new rhythm with symptoms (possible atrial fibrillation), Aisha’s emotional reluctance, a request to accept more work during orientation, a high-alert infusion, and a preceptor modeling a skipped double-check.

Apply EI: Aisha names her feeling (“I’m avoiding him because he was rude”) and separates it from the data. A symptomatic new rhythm takes priority regardless of the client’s behavior; she goes to assess him now—vital signs, symptoms, a rhythm strip—and notifies the provider.

Apply Benner: as an advanced beginner, Aisha recognizes recurring patterns but may still need help prioritizing competing complex demands. She tells Lou and the charge nurse that she can safely manage the new rhythm and her four clients but needs help before taking a fifth with a heparin infusion.
Apply the first rule of competence: she says, “I haven’t managed a heparin titration on my own yet. Would you help me with the first dose adjustment and do an independent double-check?”
Respond to the preceptor’s comment: respectfully, “Our policy requires an independent double-check for heparin, so let’s do it together.” Expertise does not remove the need to double-check.

Evaluate: Mr. Burke’s rhythm is reported and treated; the new admission is either assigned to an experienced nurse or co-managed with Lou, with a documented double-check; Aisha reviews the event with Lou afterward to build her prioritization skills.

check.q: Which of Aisha’s actions most directly demonstrates emotional intelligence, and which most directly demonstrates the first rule of competence?
check.a: EI: recognizing that her reluctance to enter Mr. Burke’s room came from her emotional reaction rather than the data, then assessing him promptly. First rule of competence: telling Lou she had not managed a heparin titration independently and asking for help and a double-check.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
In North Carolina, the NCBON regulates nursing under the Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.), with RN and LPN components of practice in 21 NCAC 36 .0224 and .0225. The RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment—and accepting an assignment is itself a professional decision for which the nurse is accountable. NCBON’s scope-of-practice decision tree walks a nurse through whether an activity is permitted and whether he or she has the education and competence to perform it safely; use it, along with agency policy and validated competencies, when you are floated or asked to take on an unfamiliar skill. Because NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state, a nurse may practice in other compact states on a multistate license but must meet the practice laws of the state where the client is located.

Competence and the legal system. If a client is harmed by care below the standard, North Carolina’s medical malpractice statute of limitations is generally 3 years, with a 4-year statute of repose (G.S. 1-15(c)). North Carolina is one of the few jurisdictions that retains pure contributory negligence as a defense. These facts are useful context, but the exam rule is national: practice only within your competence, ask for help, and document honestly.

Competence off duty. NC’s Good Samaritan law (G.S. 90-21.14) protects a person who gives emergency first aid or treatment without compensation unless injury results from gross negligence, wanton conduct, or intentional wrongdoing. It does not cover care given in the normal course of paid employment. Even off duty, provide only care within your training. Fitness for duty: impairment on duty is a conduct issue reported to NCBON, and NCBON offers alternative-to-discipline programs for nurses with substance use disorders—a path that protects the public while supporting recovery.
bullets: When floated, compare the assignment with your validated competencies; use the NCBON scope-of-practice decision tree and agency policy.
Good Samaritan protection applies to uncompensated emergency care, not to your paid shift.
A nurse who suspects a colleague is impaired reports it through the supervisor/chain of command; impairment is a Board-reportable conduct issue in NC.

sections.body: Source: Module 42 study guide, Glossary terms 4–5 (Competence, Emotional Intelligence), “Exemplar 42.A: Competence — Core Areas & Benner’s Model,” Box 42.3, Safety Alert, Focus on Diversity and Culture (pp. 2710–2712), Case Study 3: Tyree Campbell (p. 2712), and Review & Relate “Linking Competence to Legal Issues/Ethics” (p. 2712). Added national content: ethical principles, independent double-checks for high-alert medications, patient abandonment, use of qualified medical interpreters, and cultural humility.
bullets: Benner citation: the course cites Benner (2001); that is the commemorative edition of From Novice to Expert, first published in 1984. The year ranges (2–3 years for competent, 3–5 years for proficient) are approximate and refer to experience in the same or similar clinical setting; stage is setting-specific.

Floating: the course says Ms. Campbell should “refuse” the NICU assignment. Clarification: she should raise the concern before accepting report and negotiate a safe alternative (supportive tasks, buddy role, or a unit where she is competent); once a nurse has accepted clients, leaving without a proper handoff may be considered abandonment.

The IOM is now the National Academy of Medicine. The four elements of cultural competence come from the course; “cultural humility” and the use of qualified interpreters are added because they are current standards.

mnemonics.name: Benner’s stages: “Nurses Always Climb Proudly Upward to Expert”
mnemonics.text: Novice → Advanced beginner → Competent → Proficient → Expert (rules → recurring aspects → planning → wholes & maxims → intuition).

mnemonics.name: Three core areas of competence: “CPE”
mnemonics.text: Critical thinking • Problem solving (with EI) • Ethical reasoning and decision making.

mnemonics.name: Floating script: “HELP”
mnemonics.text: Help offered (“I want to help”) • Explain the gap • List the safety reason • Propose alternatives.

pearls: Competence includes knowing your limits; the safest nurse is the one who asks.
Competence is setting-specific: an expert in one specialty may be a novice in another.
Raise competence concerns before accepting report; after accepting, hand off properly before leaving.
Even experts double-check high-alert medications and sterile processes.
Emotional intelligence means noticing when feelings, not data, are driving a decision—and correcting course.
Fatigue, illness, and impairment make a skilled nurse temporarily unsafe; fitness for duty is part of competence.
Cultural competence means asking the individual and using qualified interpreters—not predicting from group membership.
redFlags: A nurse saying “I’ll figure it out as I go” or “I think this is right” about a high-risk action.
Accepting an independent assignment in a specialty (e.g., NICU, ICU, dialysis) without training or orientation.
A preceptor or expert skipping a required independent double-check for a high-alert medication.
Delaying care to a client because of personal frustration or intimidation.
Using a client’s child or family member to interpret consent or medical information.
recap: Competence = specialized knowledge, skills, abilities, and judgment, plus awareness of limits and openness to feedback.
Three core areas: critical thinking (inquire before acting), problem solving (with emotional intelligence), and ethical reasoning (ANA Code, every setting, fitness for duty).
Benner: novice (rules) → advanced beginner (recurring aspects) → competent (2–3 yrs, planning) → proficient (3–5 yrs, wholes and maxims) → expert (intuition).
Safety alert: experts still double-check; say “I don’t know”; always ask for help when unsure.
Floating beyond competence: communicate early, decline an independent assignment you can’t do safely, negotiate safe alternatives, avoid abandonment.
Cultural competence: know your own values, listen, advocate, connect to community resources; use qualified interpreters.
Lifelong competence grows through education, journals, workshops, mentorship, orientation, and collaboration—and is both a legal and an ethical duty.

checks.q: A nursing student says, “I need to follow the procedure checklist exactly; I don’t know yet when it is okay to adapt.” Which Benner stage, and is this appropriate?
checks.a: Novice. Relying on context-free rules is expected and appropriate at this stage; the student should continue to follow the procedure and ask the instructor when the situation differs.

checks.q: A float nurse realizes after accepting report that one client needs a procedure she has never performed. What should she do?
checks.a: Keep the client safe, tell the charge nurse immediately, and ask for help or for that task to be done by a competent nurse. She should not attempt the unfamiliar procedure or leave her accepted clients without a proper handoff.

checks.q: A nurse thinks, “This client is just anxious,” because the client has called repeatedly. The client now reports new chest pressure. Which competence area is at risk, and what is the action?
checks.a: Problem solving undermined by emotion (an EI failure). Assess the client immediately (vital signs, ECG per protocol, symptoms) and notify the provider—treat the new symptom objectively.

checks.q: Which statement by a nurse indicates understanding of lifelong competence: “Once I pass the NCLEX, I’m competent for my career,” or “I’ll keep up through continuing education and journals, and I’ll get orientation before working in a new specialty”?
checks.a: The second. Competence is ongoing and specialty-specific.

checks.q: A Muslim client declines a pork-derived heparin product. How does a culturally competent nurse respond?
checks.a: Respect and explore the client’s preference, notify the provider and pharmacist about the concern so alternatives can be considered, and document. The nurse advocates for the client’s wishes rather than overriding them.

checks.q: An expert nurse says, “My gut tells me this client is going downhill,” although the vital signs are within normal limits. What should a competent team do?
checks.a: Take the concern seriously: reassess thoroughly (trends, mental status, perfusion, lactate or labs per protocol), notify the provider, and consider a rapid response if criteria or concern warrant. Expert intuition is a valid cue to investigate, though it is confirmed with data.
